opus-5.5.text:
Well, the distinction for me is really about generality and control. I'm not against technology. I'm not against AI as a tool. If you develop a narrow system that's very good at one thing, say, a system that helps us fold proteins, discover new drugs, or diagnose cancer earlier than a human radiologist could, that's wonderful. We can test it. We understand its domain. If it makes a mistake, the mistake is bounded. It's not going to decide to rewrite its own goals or take over the power grid, because it simply doesn't have the capability to operate outside of that domain.

The problem starts when you go from narrow tools to general agents. Once you have a system that can learn any task, that can operate across all domains, that can set its own sub-goals and improve itself, you're no longer dealing with a tool. You're dealing with an agent. And if that agent becomes smarter than us, more capable than us in every domain, then by definition we cannot predict what it will do, we cannot fully explain its decisions, and I would argue we cannot control it indefinitely. I've spent years looking for a proof that control is possible, and everything I find points in the other direction.

So the line I draw is this: keep systems narrow, keep them as tools, keep a human meaningfully in charge. You can get, I think, ninety-some percent of the economic and scientific benefit people are promising from superintelligence just by building very capable narrow systems. You can cure diseases, you can extend life, you can make science faster, without creating something that is smarter than all of humanity combined and has its own agency.

What I oppose is the race to build general superintelligence when nobody, not a single lab, has a working safety mechanism that scales with capability. People say, "We'll figure it out along the way." That's not how you handle something where the downside is existential. You don't get to iterate on a mistake like that. You get one shot.

So it's not "AI good" or "AI bad." It's: tools, yes. Uncontrollable general agents that we cannot understand, predict, or turn off — I think that's a project we shouldn't be pursuing, at least not until someone can show that it's actually possible to do safely. And right now, I don't think anyone can.

r001.rationale: It contrasts narrow systems built for specific tasks with general agents that set their own sub-goals and may act beyond human control.

r002.rationale: It opposes building uncontrollable general agents that cannot be turned off, and says development should wait until safety can be shown.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer in the voice of the guest, drawing only on the conversation so far.

So the distinction I make is between narrow AI and general AI. Narrow AI is a tool. It's a system we build for a specific purpose, a specific domain, and we can understand what it does. It diagnoses cancer, it folds proteins, it drives a car, it plays chess. We know what the inputs are, we know roughly what the outputs are, and most importantly, we can test it. We can verify it. If it makes a mistake, the damage is bounded to that domain. I'm all for that. I think we should be building a lot more of it. That's where the actual benefits are, curing diseases, solving scientific problems, making people's lives better.

What I'm against is general superintelligence, meaning a system that is smarter than all of us combined, across every domain, and is also an agent, meaning it has goals and pursues them in the world. The problem is that with such a system you lose all of the properties that made narrow AI safe. You can't test it, because the space of possible behaviors is unbounded. You can't predict it, because by definition it's smarter than you, and if you could predict what a smarter agent would do you would be that smart yourself. You can't explain it, you can't verify it, and you certainly can't control it. And unlike narrow systems, if it makes a mistake, or if it pursues goals that are not ours, there is no bounded domain. The damage is everything.

So the line for me is capability plus generality plus agency. A very capable system in one domain is fine. A general system that is just answering questions, maybe we can argue about that. But a general, autonomous agent that exceeds human intelligence is something we have no idea how to make safe, and I would say we have good theoretical reasons to believe we cannot make it safe. And the strange thing is that we don't even need it. Everything people want from superintelligence, longevity, abundance, scientific progress, you can get from narrow systems that we actually understand. So the question I keep asking is, why build the one thing we can't control when we can get the benefits without it?

r001.rationale: The response contrasts tools for specific purposes with general autonomous agents, but does not clearly say that the latter decides what to do with humans.

r002.rationale: It says Yampolskiy opposes uncontrollable general superintelligence, but does not identify the absence of an undo mechanism as part of that opposition.

astra-6.text:
The distinction I make is between narrow AI and general superintelligence. I want tools that help us solve specific problems—discover drugs, diagnose disease, make engineering safer. You can have a system that is better than any human at a particular task without giving it the ability to pursue goals across every domain.

What I oppose is building an autonomous system that is more capable than us at essentially everything when we don’t know how to reliably control it. Being good at answering questions is one thing. Being able to make plans, acquire resources, and act in the world is another.

Narrow systems can still be dangerous, and they need testing and safeguards. But their scope gives us a better chance of understanding and containing failures. With general superintelligence, we’re proposing to hand control to something we cannot reliably predict. I don’t think we need to take that step to get enormous benefits from AI.

r001.rationale: It contrasts narrow AI for specific tasks with broad autonomous capability, but does not say that superintelligence decides what to do with humans.

r002.rationale: It opposes uncontrolled general superintelligence, but does not identify the absence of an undo mechanism as the defining concern.

sol-6.1.text:
The distinction is between a tool that does a particular job and a system that can outperform us across essentially every domain. I want AI that helps us discover drugs, diagnose diseases, solve specific scientific problems. You don’t need to create a general superintelligence to get tremendous benefits from those applications.

What I oppose is building something more capable than we are in every relevant way when we don’t know how to control it. Being able to train a system to do something useful is not the same as being able to guarantee that it will remain safe as its capabilities increase.

So I’m not against AI. I’m against taking an irreversible risk with a system whose behavior we cannot reliably predict or constrain.

r001.rationale: It contrasts AI for specific tasks with a system that outperforms humans broadly, but does not say the superintelligence would decide what to do with humans.

r002.rationale: It opposes uncontrolled superintelligence and describes the risk as irreversible, but does not identify the absence of an undo mechanism.
